description.value: The study investigated how schizophrenia and chronic cannabis use interact to affect reward anticipation sensitivity using behavioural reaction-time and directional-accuracy measures and fMRI during a reward task.

design.value: A 2 × 2 between-group design compared cannabis users and non-users among healthy controls and schizophrenia patients, with reward condition manipulated within subjects. Participants completed a two-choice reaction-time task incorporating elements of the MID and Eriksen flanker tasks while being scanned using fMRI.

task_description.value: A two-choice RT task was used with elements of the MID and Eriksen flanker tasks. Participants responded to a series of five arrow heads appearing for a fixed period, with their right or left index finger, in accordance with the pointing direction of the central arrowhead.

instructions.value: The participant was informed that the aim of the task was to gain a maximal amount of points and in order for them to win (+) or avoid losing (–), they must respond both accurately and quickly.

stimuli.value: Only the incongruent configuration of the arrow heads was used (< < > < < or > > < > >). A valence cue was either + (win), − (lose) or * (neutral), followed by a magnitude cue representing the amount of the upcoming reward (high: 20, low: 5, or none: 0).

description.value: Functional MR images were acquired using echo-planar imaging with 2 s repetition time, 36 slices and 3 × 3 × 3 mm voxel size.

description.value: A high-resolution T1 anatomical image with 1 × 1 × 1 mm voxel size was acquired for each participant.

Pre-processing was performed by spatially realigning the raw images, temporal interpolation was completed to correct for delay in slice acquisition, images were segmented using the T1 image, normalized to standard MNI space and smoothed with an 8 mm FWHM Gaussian kernel. A high-pass filter of 128 s cut off was applied.

model_settings.value: Three regressors, reward (+), punishment (−) and neutral (*), were included for the valence model. Five regressors (−20, −5, 0, +5, +20) were included for the magnitude model. Additional regressors included motion correction parameters estimated from the realignment step. T-contrasts were calculated.

A validation ROI analysis used one-sample t-tests for each contrast. The main analysis was a 2 × 2 ANCOVA assessing modulation of each contrast with cannabis use, schizophrenia status and their interaction, with years of education and age as covariates. Small-volume correction used family-wise error correction at p < 0.05 within predefined ROIs.

A 2 × 2 × 5 ANCOVA design used reward condition as the within-subject repeated measures factor and cannabis use and schizophrenia as between-group fixed factors, with education level and age as continuous covariates. Contrast values were analysed in a GLM 2 × 2 ANCOVA with cannabis use and schizophrenia as fixed factors and years of education and age as continuous covariates.
